annotations.text:
Pick a direction — then I'll build it out properly.

Same screen, same content in all four, so the only variable is the design. Each direction takes a different position on what LocalChat *is*; they are not three shades of one idea.

The chat screen only for now. Documents, Models and Settings follow once a direction is settled.

TODAY — what's there now

Bootstrap 5 defaults plus a #667eea → #764ba2 gradient, shadows and hover-lifts on every card and button, four status badges in the top bar, and boxes nested three deep (card → border → transcript).

What's actually wrong: the gradient and the drop shadows are decoration doing no work, and the nesting means four borders compete for attention before you reach a word of the answer. Your instinct is right.

A · QUIET UTILITY — Instrument Sans, cool near-white, one muted teal

The case: hierarchy from type and whitespace, nothing else. No cards, no shadows, no gradients — hairlines separate, and the reading column is capped so the answer is comfortable to read. Nav and conversations merge into one rail; the four badges become a single status line. Citations are numbered footnotes.

The tradeoff: it is quiet to the point of plain. There is no single memorable thing about it, and it will look like a lot of well-made modern tools.

B · TERMINAL — JetBrains Mono + IBM Plex Sans, warm near-black, amber

The case: this is a local-first tool for people who run their own model. It leans into that instead of hiding it — mono for every label, a prompt caret on the composer, bracketed [1] citations, a tmux-style status bar along the bottom, square corners throughout. Distinctive and hard to mistake for anything else.

The tradeoff: it takes a side. Non-technical users may read it as intimidating, and it is the hardest of the three to extend to Settings and Documents without looking gimmicky.

C · EDITORIAL — Newsreader + Instrument Sans, warm paper, oxblood

The case: the product is answers grounded in your documents, so the answer is set like a printed page — serif body at a real reading size, and citations moved out to a true margin column instead of being crammed under the text as badges. It makes the sourcing the most visible thing on screen.

The tradeoff: the margin column costs horizontal space and needs a real answer at a fallback layout on narrow screens. Serif body type in an app is a strong opinion some people simply dislike.
